brief.topic: A Small Subtraction Finds an Edge

s01: A computer can find these boundaries with subtraction.
Look at one row of this simple image.
The numbers are pixel intensities: two in the dark region, eight in the light region.
Take two neighbors, and subtract the left value from the right.
Two minus two gives zero.
At the first boundary, eight minus two gives six.
Inside the light strip, eight minus eight gives zero.
At the other boundary, two minus eight gives negative six.
The same little rule works at every position.
We can write it as two weights: negative one and positive one.
Multiply each pixel by its weight, then add.
Reusing these weights makes a map of local changes.
Move the light strip one pixel to the right.
Both boundary responses move one place too.
The rule did not need a separate version for each location.
Now add one to every pixel intensity.
Three and nine replace two and eight.
The difference is still six.
An equal addition cancels in this filter; it does not change the contrast.
This sliding multiply and sum is cross correlation, the operation commonly called convolution in neural networks.
Here we chose the weights by hand.
A trained network learns many filters from data.
One small subtraction detects a change; recognizing an object requires much more.

scenes.narration:
A computer can find these boundaries with subtraction. Look at one row of this simple image. The numbers are pixel intensities: two in the dark region, eight in the light region.

Take two neighbors, and subtract the left value from the right. Two minus two gives zero. At the first boundary, eight minus two gives six. Inside the light strip, eight minus eight gives zero. At the other boundary, two minus eight gives negative six.

The same little rule works at every position. We can write it as two weights: negative one and positive one. Multiply each pixel by its weight, then add. Reusing these weights makes a map of local changes.

Move the light strip one pixel to the right. Both boundary responses move one place too. The rule did not need a separate version for each location.

Now add one to every pixel intensity. Three and nine replace two and eight. The difference is still six. An equal addition cancels in this filter; it does not change the contrast.

This sliding multiply and sum is cross correlation, the operation commonly called convolution in neural networks. Here we chose the weights by hand. A trained network learns many filters from data. One small subtraction detects a change; recognizing an object requires much more.
